title: The Ledger of the Palatinate
premise: In 1870, as Prussian forces sweep through the Palatinate, Freya Delacroix tends the wounded in a requisitioned convent hospital and secretly records in her ledger the names of soldiers and civilians that official reports erase. When a Prussian quartermaster confiscates all town records—including her ledger—to build a sanitized archive for the victors' historians, Freya realizes the book is both evidence and death sentence: it names officers who abandoned their wounded. She joins forces with a disgraced Prussian archivist, Elias Brandt, who begins to doubt his own empire's paper truth, and together they race to copy and smuggle the ledger out before the century's official history hardens into stone. The story ends with Freya testifying before a joint Franco-German commission in 1899, the ledger admitted as record, and her found family—the surviving nurses, Elias, and an orphaned boy she saved—gathered in the rebuilt convent as the names are read aloud.
about_author: Quentin Okafor is a former military archivist turned novelist who writes about the paperwork of war—the ledgers, manifests, and omissions that decide whose lives count. He lives in Lisbon with his partner and an unruly collection of nineteenth-century field notebooks.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Fingernails
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In the convent hospital at Landau, Freya treats French and German wounded alike while quietly recording in her ledger the names no report includes—a Bavarian drummer boy, a laundress killed by stray shellfire. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: she keeps busy hands so no one asks about busy eyes.

chapters.title: The Requisition
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Prussian troops occupy the town; Captain Vogel requisitions the convent, its stores, and by clerical accident, every written record within it. Freya watches soldiers crate her ledger with parish registers and death rolls. The beat is dread disguised as compliance—she smiles, curtsies, and starts planning.

chapters.title: The Man Who Files Grief
chapters.summary: Elias Brandt's POV. A Prussian archivist arrives to organize the confiscated records into a triumphal archive. Elias, once punished for questioning casualty figures, notices the ledger's second hand—two different inks, two different truths. The beat is uneasy recognition: he has met this kind of honesty before, in himself.

chapters.title: What the Wounded Remember
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya cultivates Elias under the pretense of retrieving medicine requisitions, trading small verifiable details from the ledger to test him. Meanwhile Sister Anselma and the orphaned boy Jakob become her improvised family. The beat is calculated trust turning into something warmer than strategy.

chapters.title: Names That Cost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Elias confirms the ledger exposes Colonel Hartmann's abandonment of a field station at Weissenburg—and that Hartmann now sits on the commission writing the war's official history. Copying the ledger becomes treason. The beat is the price becoming explicit: exposure means prison or worse for them both.

chapters.title: The Convent Burns Halfway
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A fire—accident or reprisal—destroys the west wing and half the archived records. In the chaos, Freya retrieves the original ledger but loses Sister Anselma, who dies shielding the copying work. The beat is grief weaponized: mourning converts hesitation into resolve.

chapters.title: Two Hands, One Page
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias and Freya finish the duplicate ledger by lamplight, forging archival authentication stamps so it will survive scrutiny. Vogel grows suspicious and sets a trap, announcing the records will be shipped to Berlin early. The beat is intimacy forged under pressure—two liars telling the same truth.

chapters.title: The Cart to Zweibrücken
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Smuggling the duplicate out hidden beneath Jakob's coffin in a burial cart, Freya faces Vogel at the gate; Elias covers her with falsified manifests, sacrificing his career on the spot. The cart passes. The beat is terror transfigured into release—they are committed, visible, undone and free.

chapters.title: Hartmann's History
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Vogel arrests Elias; Hartmann moves to bury everything as forgery. Freya, instead of fleeing, walks into the commission's temporary headquarters and demands her testimony be entered on the record, producing matching ink samples and witness affidavits. The beat is the climax: invisibility abandoned, one nurse against an empire's narrative.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, 1899. Before the joint commission, the ledger is authenticated and entered into the historical record; Hartmann resigns in disgrace, and Elias, released, joins Freya as the names are read aloud in the rebuilt convent. Jakob, nearly grown, reads the last page. The beat is inheritance: the ledger passes to the next generation, and survival finally means being remembered.
